question.text: As ruler, Tutankhamun reversed the religious reforms of his father, Akhenaten. One such reform moved his capital from Akhetaten to this city on the east bank of the Nile near the Valley of the Kings.
question.clue: Troops from this city employed the "cutting off the snake's head" technique to defeat Cleombrotus of Sparta.

swap.leadin: Identify some of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
swap.text: This triangular tomb of Khufu ("KOO-foo") stands in a necropolis on the outskirts of Cairo. The Great Sphinx stands nearby.
swap.clue: Slave labor was long thought to have been used to build this structure, but many archaeologists believe that thousands of skilled laborers were used instead over a 20 year period.

question.text: The discovery of this pharaoh's tomb was monumental because it was nearly fully intact, with very few artifacts stolen by grave robbers. Howard Carter discovered the tomb of this pharaoh, the youngest ruler of Egypt.
question.clue: This pharaoh moved Egypt's capital back to Thebes from Amarna and reinstated the worship of traditional Egyptian gods.

swap.text: This last pharaoh of Ancient Egypt unsuccessfully allied herself with Mark Antony and committed suicide, supposedly by an asp bite, in 30 BCE.
swap.clue: The servant Eros was instructed to kill a lover of this ruler before that lover declared he was "grieved that a commander as great as I should be found to be inferior to a woman in courage."

question.leadin: This city was built on the site of the ancient city of Rhacotis.
question.text: Name this city, the largest in the world by 200 BCE. The Musaeum, an academic institution based in this city, was the source of the modern word "museum" and also encompassed this city's famous Great Library.
question.clue: A journey south from this city to Syene was used to create an arc measurement that produced an estimate of 250,000 stadia.

swap.leadin: Answer the following questions about the Diadochi.
swap.text: This diadochus was given control of Egypt after Alexander's death, starting a namesake Greco-Egyptian dynasty that lasted until Cleopatra. He shares his name with a later mathematician from Alexandria.
swap.clue: This person had Cleomenes of Naucratis killed supposedly since he was "a friend of Perdiccas, and therefore no friend of his".

question.text: Ships traveling long distances in the ancient world stopped at the Himyarite site of Muza on this body of water. The Aksumite kingdom also used their papyrus-sailed ships to guard ports on this sea.
question.clue: The Hejaz abuts this sea which the Bab el-Mandeb links to the Gulf of Aden.

swap.text: This ruler of the Third Dynasty had his architect Imhotep constructed a step pyramid for him, the first of the Egyptian pyramids.
swap.clue: An official of this pharaoh communes with the god Khnum to stop a seven-year flood, as recorded on the Famine Stela.

question.text: The Story of Sinuhe ("sin-NOO-hay") references the murder of Amenemhat I, a ruler of this Egyptian kingdom that ruled between the first two Intermediate Periods.
question.clue: The fnal rulers of this period were called the Xois Dynasty since they moved the capital there.

swap.text: The 1274 BCE Battle of Kadesh was not Ramses's first time fighting over Kadesh. In 1306 BCE, Ramses joined this man, his father, in a victory over the Hittites which briefly seized the city for Egypt.
swap.clue: The father of Ramses II, he built a temple at Abydos decorated with a series of famous reliefs.

question.text: After the battle ended in a draw, Muwatalli II signed the world's earliest known peace treaty with this Egyptian pharaoh. The Abu Simbel temples were constructed by this "great" pharaoh.
question.answerHtml: Ramesses II(RAM-a-sees the second) [or Ramesses the Great, or Ozymandias, prompt on “Ramesses”]
question.clue: This ruler concluded the first documented peace treaty after fighting the inconclusive Battle of Kadesh against the Hittite Empire.

swap.text: This Alexandrian mathematician wrote a commentary on Diophantus' Arithmetica. This Neoplatonist philosopher and pagan was killed after she advised the governor Orestes in his feud with Patriarch Cyril.
swap.clue: Her only known work is a commentary on Book III of her father, Theon's, edition of Ptolemy's Almagest although she may have worked on his edition of 's Elements as well.

question.leadin: Josephus claimed that these people founded Jerusalem and gave a false etymology for their name deriving from the Greek for "Shepherd-kings."
question.text: Name these people whose name comes from the ancient Egyptian for "rulers of foreign lands." These people's 15th Dynasty ruled from Avaris during the Second Intermediate Period.
question.clue: Their capital was at Avaris, and they were overthrown by Ahmose.

swap.leadin: A ceremonial macehead belonging to this ruler shows them enthroned under a canopy, wearing the Red Crown, though it likely does not depict a Sed-festival.
swap.text: Name this ruler who, on one side of a namesake palette made around 3000 BCE, is depicted wearing the White crown, about to kill a prisoner. This ruler's name is written in a serekh with the symbols for a catfish and chisel.
swap.clue: The existence of this pharaoh is attested to by a namesake palette that depicts him with two crowns. This pharaoh was the unifier of Upper and Lower Egypt.

question.leadin: Identify the following about a certain Egyptian pharaoh.
question.text: This pharaoh of the Fourth Dynasty loved to build pyramids, constructing not only the failed pyramid at Huni and the Bent Pyramid, but also what may be the first successful smooth pyramid, the Red Pyramid at Dahshur.
question.clue: This ruler was married to Hetepheres I, and he likely built the Praise of the Two Lands ship.

swap.text: This statue at Giza depicts a half-animal, half-lion figure. Napoleon was falsely accused of breaking this statue's nose with a cannonball.

question.leadin: This city was a cult center for the ram god Heryshaf.
question.text: Name this Ancient Egyptian city south of the Fayum that dominated Lower Egypt during the First Intermediate Period, in opposition to Thebes in the north. Mentuhotep II (men-TOO-hoh-tep "the second") conquered this city to reunify Egypt into the Middle Kingdom.

swap.leadin: Paul of Aegina's ("ee-JYE-nuh's") medical compendium cites a cosmetic text by a physician identified with this ruler, who was credited with medieval writings on pessaries and alchemy like the Chrysopoeia ("kry-so-PEE-uh").
swap.text: Name this ruler who cuts open the wombs of enslaved women to study sexual differentiation in a story from the Talmud. This ruler supposedly cured baldness with bear's grease and dissolved a pearl in vinegar.
swap.answerHtml: Cleopatra [or Cleopatra VII or Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator; accept “Cleopatra the Physician” or “Cleopatra the Alchemist”]
swap.clue: This person was successful after Ptolemy ordered the death of Pompey the Great, which led to Julius Caesar supporting this person.

question.leadin: This woman invented an early double-boiler, now culinarily referred to as this woman's namesake bath.
question.text: Identify this first-century woman, who Zosimos of Panopolis regarded as the first alchemist in the Western world. She is known for a namesake alchemical axiom stating "One becomes two, two becomes three, and out of the third comes the one as the fourth."
question.answerHtml: Mary the Jewess [accept Mary the Prophetess; accept Maria the Copt; accept Maria Hebraea; accept Maria Prophetissa; accept Māriyya al-Qibṭiyya; prompt on Mary alone]

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the end of the Old Kingdom, FTPE.
swap.text: Toward the very end of the Old Kingdom, the Pyramid Texts began to be replaced by these religious texts, as exemplified by discoveries at the Balat necropolis. In general, they made the afterlife more accessible to commoners than the Pyramid Texts.
